title: Keep turning back to Him, and keep praying.
subtitle: How to hold on to the fitrah
then: Ibn Kathir explains turning to Him as {idea}returning to Him{/idea}, and mindfulness as remembering He is always watching. Prayer is {reward}the greatest act of worship.{/reward} When 'Umar asked Mu'adh about the foundation of this Ummah, he named sincerity, prayer, and obedience. 'Umar said, {idea}you have spoken the truth.{/idea}
now: You drift. A busy week, missed prayers, a habit creeps back. {trap}Then shame says it is pointless to start again.{/trap} {idea}The verse uses the word for turning back, over and over.{/idea} Coming back is the whole method, not a failure of it.
old: I have slipped too many times to keep coming back.
new: Turning back is what I was told to keep doing. Every return counts.
try: Pray your next prayer on time, with the intention of returning to Allah.

title: They split their religion, each group pleased with itself.
subtitle: The trap of smug factions

row.title: the Prophet's way
sub: what he and his Companions were upon

then: Ibn Kathir explains that those who split their religion {trap}believed in parts of it and rejected other parts{/trap}, each group claiming the truth. Asked which group would be saved, the Prophet ﷺ answered: {idea}what I and my Companions are upon.{/idea}
now: The argument in the community chat about whose mosque is right. The eye-roll at someone who prays a little differently. {trap}The quiet pleasure of being in the correct group.{/trap} {idea}The verse turns you to the Prophet's way, and away from pride in your own circle.{/idea}
old: My group has it right. The others are the problem.
new: Pride in my faction is the trap. My task is to follow the Prophet's way humbly.
try: Next time you feel superior to another Muslim's practice, make dua for them and for yourself instead.

title: In trouble they call Him alone. In ease, they forget.
subtitle: The swing between need and neglect
then: Ibn Kathir describes how people sway. {trap}In dire straits they call on Allah alone{/trap}, sincerely. Then times of ease come, and some go back to worshipping others alongside Him. {idea}The verse holds up a mirror to that swing.{/idea}
now: Your child had a fever of 40 and you prayed all night. A month later, healthy and laughing, {trap}your prayer is rushed and your mind elsewhere.{/trap} {idea}The One who answered in the night is the One who keeps her well now.{/idea}
old: I pray hardest when I need something. That is just human.
new: Allah is not only for emergencies. The ease is also from Him.
try: Make one dua today when nothing is wrong, just thanking Allah for a calm moment.

title: Enjoy for now. You will come to know.
subtitle: A warning from the One who says Be
then: Ibn Kathir quotes one of the early scholars: {idea}if a law officer said this to me, I would be afraid.{/idea} So what about when the warning comes from the One who only says to a thing Be, and it is? The ingratitude is {trap}enjoying the gift while denying the Giver.{/trap}
now: A traffic officer says you will hear about this, and your stomach drops for days. {trap}Yet the Quran's warnings slide past us.{/trap} {idea}The verse asks you to feel the weight of who is speaking.{/idea}
old: Warnings in the Quran are general, not really for me.
new: If I fear a human warning, I should take Allah's far more seriously.
try: Read this verse once more slowly, and name one gift you have been enjoying without thanks.

title: Where is your proof? Did We send it down?
subtitle: Worship without evidence
then: Ibn Kathir explains this is {idea}a rhetorical question to denounce them{/idea}. Did Allah send them any proof that speaks for what they worship? {trap}They have no such thing.{/trap} They worshipped others with no evidence at all.
now: A forwarded message tells you to read a special dua 40 times for a miracle. A relative insists on a ritual because grandma did it. {trap}It is easy to follow without asking where it came from.{/trap} {idea}The verse asks: what is the proof?{/idea}
old: If it is part of tradition, it must be right.
new: My worship should rest on what Allah revealed, not on habit.
try: Pick one religious habit you do and find out its source this week.

title: Joy turns to pride, hardship turns to despair.
subtitle: The believer's middle path
then: Ibn Kathir says this describes people {trap}proud when given blessings, despairing when hardship comes{/trap}. Except those who are patient in difficulty and do good in ease. He cites the hadith: {idea}how wonderful is the affair of the believer{/idea}, who gives thanks in good times and is patient in bad, {reward}and both are good for him.{/reward}
now: The bonus comes and you feel on top of the world, telling everyone. Next week the car breaks down and you feel nothing will ever go right. {trap}The swing exhausts you.{/trap} {idea}Thanks in the good, patience in the bad: both keep you steady.{/idea}
old: When things go well, I am great. When they go badly, it is hopeless.
new: Good times call for thanks, hard times for patience. Both can be good for me.
try: Today, thank Allah for one good thing and ask patience for one hard thing.

title: He widens provision for some and narrows it for others.
subtitle: A reason not to swing between pride and despair
then: Right after the swing of joy and despair, this verse. Ibn Kathir says {idea}He is the One controlling it{/idea}, by His wisdom and justice, expanding for some and restricting for some. {reward}In that are signs for people who believe.{/reward}
now: A slow month at the shop. A colleague's side business takes off. {trap}You either blame yourself or feel cheated.{/trap} {idea}Your share is measured by His wisdom{/idea}, which means neither the full months nor the lean ones are the final story.
old: How much I have is all down to me.
new: I work, and Allah measures. That frees me from both pride and despair.
try: On your next payday, say: this is from Allah, whatever the amount.

title: Give your relatives, the poor, and the traveler their due.
subtitle: Giving as a right, not a favor
then: Ibn Kathir explains the relative's due as {idea}respect and keeping the ties of kinship{/idea}. The needy are those with nothing, or not enough. The traveler is the one in need on the road. All this for those seeking {reward}Allah's Face, to look upon Him on the Day of Resurrection.{/reward}
now: The cousin you have not called in two years. The neighbor who is quietly struggling since the layoff. The stranger at the station short on fare. {idea}The verse calls what you give them their right{/idea}, not your favor.
old: Helping family and strangers is extra, if I can spare it.
new: What I give my relatives and those in need is already theirs by right.
try: Call one relative you have lost touch with today, just to ask how they are.

title: Giving to get more back does not grow with Allah.
subtitle: What multiplies and what does not
then: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others explained this as {trap}a gift given in the hope of getting back more{/trap}. There is no reward for it with Allah. But what is given seeking His Face is multiplied. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith: {reward}a date given from lawful earnings grows until it is like Mount Uhud.{/reward}
now: The wedding gift you size up by what they gave you last time. The favor done for a colleague because you will need one back. {trap}It is a quiet trade.{/trap} {idea}The verse invites a different kind of giving{/idea}: small, honest, for Allah alone, and watched over by Him.
old: When I give, I expect something back.
new: What I give hoping for a return stays small. What I give for Allah grows.
try: Give one small thing today to someone who cannot pay you back.

title: He created, provides, ends your life, and revives you.
subtitle: Four acts no partner can do
then: Ibn Kathir describes how a person is brought from the womb {idea}naked and knowing nothing{/idea}, unable to see or hear, with no strength. Then Allah gives him everything: clothing, wealth, earnings. He causes death and gives life again. {trap}None of the partners people worship can do any of it.{/trap}
now: Your first salary, your first flat, your own kitchen. It feels like you built it all. {idea}Trace it back: you arrived with nothing, not even sight.{/idea} The verse asks you to see who has carried you from that cot to this desk.
new: From my first breath to my last, it is Allah who provides and sustains.
try: Look around your room tonight and name five things you did not have when you were born.

title: Corruption spreads by people's hands, so they might return.
subtitle: When sin shows up in the world around us
then: Scholars gave various meanings: withheld rain and famine, killing on land and piracy at sea. Abu Al-'Aliyah said: {idea}whoever disobeys Allah on earth has corrupted it{/idea}, because the earth's good depends on obedience. Ibn Kathir says Allah lets them taste part of it {reward}so they may return.{/reward}
now: The lie at work that poisons trust in the whole team. The shouting at home that makes the kids anxious. {trap}Small wrongs spread beyond us.{/trap} {idea}The verse says each harm we taste is also a door: perhaps they will return.{/idea}
old: My small wrongs only affect me.
new: What my hands do spreads. And every bitter taste is an invitation to turn back.
try: Think of one wrong habit whose effect spreads to others. Stop it for today.

title: Travel and see how those before ended up.
subtitle: History as a mirror
then: After describing corruption on land and sea, the Prophet ﷺ is told to say: travel and look. Ibn Kathir says, {idea}see what happened to them{/idea} when they rejected the messengers and {trap}were ungrateful for the blessings.{/trap} Most of them were associators.
now: You visit a museum full of empires that once seemed eternal. You read about a family business that collapsed after one generation of greed. {idea}The verse turns sightseeing into reflection.{/idea} What would someone learn from your story?
new: History is a mirror. Their ending warns me about my own choices.
try: Next time you see ruins or read about a fallen power, ask one question about your own gratitude.

title: Set your face to the right way before that Day comes.
subtitle: Hurry to good, while there is time
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah here {idea}commands His servants to hasten to obey Him and to do good deeds{/idea}. When He wills the Day to come, {trap}no one can avert it{/trap}. Then people will be divided into two groups.
now: I will get serious about prayer after exams. After the wedding. After the kids grow up. {trap}The list never ends.{/trap} {idea}The verse says: before.{/idea} Before the Day nobody can push back. Today is already before.
old: I will sort out my faith when life settles down.
new: The time to turn is now, while turning is still possible.
try: Pick one good thing you keep postponing and do the first step of it today.

title: Doing good is preparing a bed for yourself.
subtitle: Every deed lands back on its doer

row.title: disbelief
sub: weighs on the one who chose it

then: The verse right after the division of people. Ibn Kathir explains: {trap}whoever disbelieves will suffer from it{/trap}, and whoever does good {reward}prepares a good place for themselves.{/reward} {idea}Each deed lands back on the one who did it.{/idea}
now: You make your bed in the morning and come home to it tired and grateful. {idea}Every good deed is like that, smoothing a place you will rest in.{/idea} The prayer at dawn, the kind word, the hidden charity: you are setting up your own room.
old: Good deeds are sacrifices I make for others.
new: Every good deed is me preparing my own resting place.
try: Do one quiet good deed today and think: I am preparing my place.

title: The reward comes from His bounty, not our math.
subtitle: One good deed, ten to seven hundred times over
then: Ibn Kathir explains: He rewards believers {reward}from His bounty{/reward}, ten times for one good deed, up to seven hundred, as much as He wills. {trap}He does not love the disbelievers{/trap}, yet He is still just with them and does not wrong them.
now: You gave five dollars at the mosque and felt it was nothing. You helped an elderly man with his bags and forgot it by lunch. {idea}Allah has not forgotten.{/idea} {reward}His reward is not a receipt. It is bounty.{/reward}
old: My good deeds are too small to matter.
new: Allah multiplies from His bounty. No sincere deed is too small.
try: Do one tiny good deed today, a smile, a text of thanks, and trust Allah to grow it.
